summary: Documents experiences with the RFC 1797 experiment in subnetting a class A network, run by the Net39 Test Group, and gives recommendations to the Internet registries and the operations community. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The report after the cake-slicing test: what went wrong and what to do next.

subtitle: What happened when part of a Class A network was carved into subnets, and what routers needed to cope.

tldr.problem: Class A address space had not been split into smaller subnets across providers, and it was unclear whether routers and operations would cope.
tldr.mechanism: The Net39 Test Group delegated subnets under the RFC 1797 experiment, ran common services over them, and recorded routing, DNS and operational problems.
tldr.outcome: The memo calls the experiment a success and says it is safe to start carving up Class A space if delegated by normal Internet Registry conventions, and recommends IANA consider this.

today: RFC 1879 is an Informational memo with no obsoleting or updating RFC listed. It reports on the experiment defined in RFC 1797.

sections.title: The RFC 1797 Experiment
sections.content:
This memo records experiences with the RFC 1797 subnet A experiment, performed by the Net39 Test Group. Not all proposed experiments were done: only the "case one" delegations were made. Extra testing covered DNS, with a root nameserver and the primary for the domain inside the subnetted space, and classless delegation.

Services run over the experiment included Finger, HTTP, Telnet, FTP, Gopher, kerberos, lpr, X and DNS. F.Root-Servers.Net had an interface in the experiment: its operator reported 400,000,000 queries in 38 days, well over half to the temporary 39.13.229.241 address, and he kept the old 192.5.5.241 address so stale root.cache files would not create a black hole.
sections.plainLanguage: A test was run where one huge block of addresses was split up and shared. Real services like web and email were run on it, including a very busy DNS server.

sections.title: Operational Problems
sections.content:
Early predictions said the safest path for a provider was to have all clients either singly connected to one upstream provider or running a classless interior routing protocol. A network with a default route may not notice a problem until it starts using subnets of traditional Class A networks internally.

At least one RIPE181 implementation had initial problems. Operators need to register all active aggregates and delegations in the Internet Routing Registry (IRR), and there need to be ways to find who may announce a prefix.

Traceroute using loose source routing (LSRR) was critical for troubleshooting. In cisco IOS, no ip source-route disables LSRR and so hinders cross-provider troubleshooting; the memo recommends not putting it in active ISP configurations. It also says there are serious weaknesses in the inter-provider cooperation model, which it leaves outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbouring network companies must write down who owns which slice, and must keep their debugging tools turned on so they can help each other find problems.

sections.title: Routing Problems and Fixes
sections.content:
A classic cisco setup that redistributes a static route like 39.1.28.0 255.255.255.0 into BGP will, by default, promote a classful subnet route to a full classful route. The memo shows two ways around this, including no auto-summary. Users also need ip classless and ip subnet-zero: the first removes the idea that knowing a subnet means knowing the whole network, and the second is needed because it is no longer clear where the all-ones or all-zeros networks are.

Equipment relying on classful protocols such as RIPv1 was prone to misconfiguration. An Ascend told to announce 39.1.28/24 sent 39/8 instead because RIPv1 cannot carry the longer prefix. The memo says RIPv1 and all classful IGPs should be considered historic.

For the unintended aggregation, the preferred fix is ip classless plus a default route inside the AS, which works only for single-homed ISPs. Workarounds for software 9.1 or later and 9.0 or older rely on manual configuration that the memo says will be impossible to maintain in the long run.
sections.plainLanguage: Some older machines only understood whole big blocks, so when asked to announce a small slice, they announced the entire block. Newer settings teach routers to handle small slices.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
The memo concludes that the RFC 1797 experiment appears to have been a success. It believes it safe to start carving up Class A space if the spaces are delegated according to normal Internet Registry conventions, and recommends that IANA consider this for future address delegations.

Its Security Considerations section says security issues were not considered in this experiment.
sections.plainLanguage: The report's answer is yes, you can slice up the big blocks, as long as you follow the usual rules for handing them out.
